ai.description: The Castle Rock Night Frog reaches 25–30 mm. It is brown with a pale snout and granular skin. Distinctive features include a prominent, pointed snout and flattened body adapted for rock crevices.
ai.identificationRemarks: *Nyctibatrachus petraeus* is uniquely distinguished by its distinctively pointed, protruding snout and a prominent, fleshy tubercle located at the tip of the rostrum.
ai.habitat: The Castle Rock Night Frog inhabits high-altitude evergreen forests in the Western Ghats, typically found near rocky streams at elevations between 600 and 1,000 meters.
ai.behavior: The Castle Rock Night Frog is strictly nocturnal, remaining hidden in rock crevices during the day and emerging at night to forage for small invertebrates along stream banks.
ai.reproductionNotes: *Nyctibatrachus petraeus* breeds during the monsoon, laying clutches of 15–30 eggs on wet rocks. It exhibits direct development, bypassing the free-swimming tadpole stage.
ai.distributionRemarks: *Nyctibatrachus petraeus* is endemic to the southern Western Ghats in Kerala, India, typically found at high elevations between 1,000 and 1,500 meters.
ai.callDescription: The Castle Rock Night Frog emits a series of high-pitched, insect-like chirps while perched on wet, mossy rocks near fast-flowing streams in the Western Ghats.
